title: Nandamuri Balakrishna, Sunny Deol, Nayanthara Lead Zee Studios’ Multilingual 2026-27 Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
description: India’s Zee Studios has unveiled a diversified multilingual, multi-genre content slate for 2026-27, spanning Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil, Malayala
body:
India’s Zee Studios has unveiled a diversified multilingual, multi-genre content slate for 2026-27, spanning Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Gujarati and Kannada cinema. 

	The portfolio brings together commercial entertainers, action spectacles, thrillers, mythology-driven epics and regionally rooted stories.

	On the Hindi-language side, the slate includes “Baap,” starring Sunny Deol, Sanjay Dutt, Jackie Shroff and Mithun Chakraborty, directed by Vivek Singh Chauhan. “Shri Ram Bhoomi,” starring Anupam Kher, Ritwik Bhowmik and Amruta Khanvilkar and directed by Kamakhya Narayan Singh, draws on Indian mythology and history. Other Hindi titles include “Delhi 2021,” starring Richa Chadha and directed by Abhishek Acharya; “Blind Babu,” starring Nawazuddin Siddiqui and directed by Ravi Varma; and “Blind Game,” starring Arjun Rampal and Priyamani and directed by Sangeeth Sivan.
	

	The Telugu-language slate features a project currently identified “NBK111,” starring Nandamuri Balakrishna and directed by Gopichand Malineni, and “Indraputra,” starring Kiran Abbavaram and directed by Srikanth Puppala. Also on the slate are “Kanaka Durga,” “Anasuya General Stores” and “January 12 Vidudala,” which stars Venkatesh Daggubati, Keerthy Suresh and Kalyan Ram and is directed by Anil Ravipudi.


	In the Tamil language, the studio is backing “Hi,” starring Nayanthara and Kavin and directed by Vishnu Edavan, and “Sathyavan Savithri,” starring Keerthy Suresh and Mysskin and directed by Praveen S. Vijaay. The Kannada-language entry “Anna From Mexico” stars Dhananjaya, Reeshma Nanaiah, Umashree, Rangayana Raghu and Sadhu Kokila under director Shankar Guru. Zee Studios has also stepped into the Gujarati-language market with “Tom and Cherry,” starring Siddharth Randeria and Dhanya Doshi and directed by Dharmessh Mehta.
	

	Marathi-language  cinema forms another pillar of the strategy, building on the Indian National Film Award-winning “Aatmapamphlet.” The new slate includes “Jhep,” directed by Priyadarshan Jadhav; “Phulwara,” starring Priyadarshini Indalkar and directed by Ravi Jadhav; “Jogai,” starring Jitendra Joshi and Sajiri Joshi and directed by Vishal Modhave; and “Maan.”

	The genre mix extends further with “Silaa,” starring Harshvardhan Rane, Sadia Khateeb and Karanveer Mehra and directed by Omung Kumar.

	Zee Studios is also set to collaborate with Anil Kapoor Film & Communication Network for the first time on “Paaltu.”

	“Our portfolio strategy is driven by the belief that India cannot be represented through one kind of story, one language or one cinematic lens,” a Zee Studios spokesperson said. “Every market has its own audience, talent, creative ecosystem and entertainment sensibility, and our ambition is to reflect that diversity through the films we back.”

	“From Hindi, Marathi, Malayalam and Gujarati to Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and other language markets, we are dedicated towards building an unconventional content ecosystem with differentiated storytelling,” the spokesperson added. “For us, entertainment serves as the backbone for multilingual and multi-genre cinema, blurring the geographical and colloquial boundaries.”

body:
Andy Garcia, Karla Souza and Wilmer Valderrama were among those on the red carpet Friday night for the 41st annual Imagen Awards at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills.
Celebrating Latino talent and creatives across entertainment, the gala honored Andy Garcia with the Lifetime Achievement Award for his four-decade career. In his acceptance speech, the “Landman” star shared this his first job upon moving to Los Angeles was at the Beverly Hilton
“I encourage you to keep dreaming and keep challenging those obstacles. Keep falling forward,” the “Landman” star said. “My father…would always say, ‘Never take a step backward, not even to gain momentum.”
Garcia closed out the evening with a live performance featuring The CineSon All Stars and Arturo Sandoval.

title: Hulu Cancels Mindy Kaling-Created Comedy ‘Not Suitable for Work’ After One Season (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Hulu will not be moving forward on a second season of its recent comedy “Not Suitable for Work,” from creator Mindy Kaling. The series, which Kaling
body:
Hulu will not be moving forward on a second season of its recent comedy “Not Suitable for Work,” from creator Mindy Kaling. The series, which Kaling executive produced with showrunner Charlie Grandy and 3 Arts Entertainment’s Howard Klein, launched in June and ran for nine episodes. Warner Bros. TV, which produces the series, plans to shop it to potential new homes.

	Ella Hunt, Avantika, Will Angus, Jack Martin, Nicholas Duvernay and Jay Ellis star in the series, which per the show’s logline, centers on “work-obsessed 20-somethings striving for professional success and, if they have time, personal happiness in Manhattan’s most glamorous neighborhood, Murray Hill.”
	

	Recurring guest stars on “Not Suitable for Work” include Victor Garber, Greg Germann, Judy Gold, Ego Nwodim, Harry Richardson, Constance Wu, Laura Bell Bundy, May Hong, Bhavesh Patel, Emilia Suárez and Michael Benjamin Washington.


	The series stars Hunt as AJ, an investment banker from Boston, who moves to New York for a new job and begins living with her best friend, aspiring celebrity stylist Abby (played by Avantika). They live across the hall from male best friends Davis (Will Angus), who is AJ’s co-worker and has a crush on her; nepo-baby/young journalist Josh (Jack Martin); and aspiring actor/med school dropout Kel (Nicholas Duvernay).

	“Not Suitable for Work” was produced under Kaling’s Kaling International label in association with Warner Bros. Television, where both Kaling and Grandy hold overall deals.

	“Not Suitable for Work” repped Kaling’s first sole creator credit on a project since “The Mindy Project,” the comedy that began its life on Fox for three seasons before moving over to Hulu, where it ran for an additional three seasons as one of the streamer’s earliest original hits. After “Mindy Project,” Kaling continued a string of successes with Netflix’s “Never Have I Ever,” HBO Max’s “The Sex Lives of College Girls” and Netflix’s ongoing series “Running Point,” which has already been renewed for a Season 3.
	

	In her review of “Not Suitable for Work,” Variety‘s Alison Herman wasn’t too impressed, but she did see some “glimmers of a more biting, memorable take on young people juggling jobs and love in New York City throughout the nine-episode season.”

schema.headline: Hulu Cancels Mindy Kaling-Created Comedy ‘Not Suitable for Work’ After One Season (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Taylor Swift Recalls How ‘I Knew You Were Trouble’ Was Written As a ‘Really Sad Ballad’ in Grammy Museum Conversation Video
description: Taylor Swift opened up about the process of writing and recording her 2012 hit “I Knew You Were Trouble,” revealing that it was initially penned as
body:
Taylor Swift opened up about the process of writing and recording her 2012 hit “I Knew You Were Trouble,” revealing that it was initially penned as a “really sad ballad” before she was encouraged to incorporate dubstep.

	Swift reflected on the song’s creation during a Q&A at the Grammy Museum in Los Angeles last week, moderated by Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. The conversation, held as part of the Museum’s Icon Sessions, included Mason Jr. asking Swift how she prefers to build production around her lyrics and storytelling to create the “right mood and vibe.”
	

#TaylorSwift reveals that “I Knew You Were Trouble” started as a “sad piano ballad” until Max Martin and Shellback suggested, “What if it’s dubstep?”Swift adds that it ended up being “the best thing” that could have happened to the song.Watch the full Grammy Museum… pic.twitter.com/q3fhTLODw9— Variety (@Variety) August 24, 2026


	“It can either be compelling to make a song sound exactly how it feels or to flip it, which the people that really taught me the most about that are Max Martin and Shellback,” said Swift in a clip from the event. The best example of this, she noted, was “I Knew You Were Trouble,” which she originally had written as a “sad piano ballad.”


	“I was really excited to bring it in and I played them this really, really sad ballad and I was like I think just no drums and they’re like, ‘What if it’s dubstep?'” she recalled. “I was like I don’t know, guys. Let’s give it a run. I don’t know.”

	Swift explained that in the end, it “ended up being the best thing for it, and I think as a collaborator, my favorite people to be in the room with are ‘Yes, and?’ people. So why not try it. If they heard it and they thought dubstep, and I came to them specifically because I didn’t want to be making lateral moves creatively, why wouldn’t we go down that path? Why wouldn’t we? I really think that enthusiasm in the studio, it can really make or break what you end up creating.”
	

	“I Knew You Were Trouble” was part of a decided shift for Swift, who embraced a more pop-oriented sound on the song’s parent album “Red.” The experimentation paid off, as “Trouble” bowed at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and inevitably reached a peak of No. 2.

title: Taylor Swift Sings Mashup of ‘All Too Well,’ ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ and ‘August’ in Grammy Museum Video
description: Most Taylor Swift fans probably do not think of the sad events of “All Too Well” and the ultimately happy “Toy Story 5” as occurring in the same cin
body:
Most Taylor Swift fans probably do not think of the sad events of “All Too Well” and the ultimately happy “Toy Story 5” as occurring in the same cinematic or musical universe. But, to the contrary, Swift sees a clear thematic connection between her epic romantic tragedy of 14 years ago and the happily-ever-after saga of Jessie in this year’s Pixar film, with some choice “Folklore” from the years in-between as connective tissue — namely, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” “August” and “All Too Well.” 
	

	The mashup of the three numbers comes as a surprise at the climax of a newly released video of a recent program at the Grammy Museum, which was released online Monday on the Recording Academy‘s YouTube channel. The fewer than 200 attendees at last week’s semi-secret session in the museum’s intimate Clive Davis Theater had done a good job of helping keep the nature of the performance under wraps until now.


	Swift introduced the six-minute solo piano performance following a 42-minute interview with Recording Academy chief Harvey Mason Jr. Speaking directly to the audience, she explained that what they were about to hear would be an echo of the surprise medleys she performed on her record-breaking stadium tour that wrapped up in December 2024.

	“This is the piano that I brought with me all around the world on the Eras Tour,” she says in the video, “and one of my favorite things that I would do on the Eras Tour and something that really became something the fans paid a lot of attention to and would make a lot of guesses about every night was, I had this section called the acoustic section. I would do different songs every night, one on guitar and one on piano, and I started to really have a blast with creating medleys towards the middle/end part of the tour. And I’d really just think about different songs I could mash up with other songs (as) kind of a surprise and delight moment for fans. And a way that I would pick the songs is, I’d find some sort of through line, whether that was rhythmically or these are all about a similar emotion. And I prepared one for you today that, if I was still on the Eras Tour, I would do this one. And it’s songs that are connected to each other by the common theme of being about memory and reliving certain detailed memories of your life and the significance of those memories.” 
	



	The strands of the three songs are interwoven in a way that makes it sometimes difficult to discern where one ends and another begins, especially as elements of the tunes are repeatedly reprised and entwined. The mashup starts with the wistful opening lines of “I Knew It, I Knew You” — “I knew you through the daze of the blades of the grass in summer / Parachutes for the free fall of being younger” — before “the rivers I cried when we said goodbye” turn to the sad strains of the breakup song “All Too Well.” Things turn sunnier again with sunny excerpts from “August,” and then, by the time the six minutes are up, the mashing has gotten more severe, with tangled lines like “I remember it, you were the free fall of being younger” and “I knew it, I knew it all too well.” 

	“I Knew It, I Knew You” continues to do well on the country chart — as well as on Billboard’s Hot 100 — and Swift spoke about resuming her romance with the genre that brought her to the dance. “I think this can happen as you grow up,” she told Mason, prior to moving to the piano. “I love my country roots more and more, the further along this path I get, and I want to honor them more and more, and I feel more tied and more loyal to them. The people that shaped who I am as an artist and as a writer, that all happened in Nashville.”

	Swift spoke at the beginning of the program about her first single, “Tim McGraw” (while offering no clues about whether a deluxe edition of her debut album might yet come to fruition, as hoped). She picked out a line that might have alluded to slightly saucier circumstances than were directly stated.

	“That song, when I look back on it,  it kind of establishes a pattern of writing in detail,” she said. “That’s something that people bring up to me a lot about my work, is that I write in detail. But I do think it’s important to determine that the details have to have a significance to the story at hand. And in that song, there’s a line that says, ‘Just a boy in a Chevy truck that has a tendency of getting stuck on back roads at night.’ And if you look at that at face value, you’re like, ‘Oh, that truck broke down a lot.’ But if you look into it, the double meaning is these are two teenagers who used to, like, park and kiss and tell their parents that the truck broke down.”
	

	“Ah. So now we know!” responded Mason.

	Moving on to her third album, “Speak Now,” Swift said, “On that album, I really learned how to take a feeling I was feeling and then craft that on my own into a sound and kind of world-build the music around my feeling for it…. The song ‘Enchanted’ is about falling in love and that sort of glittery, twinkly fairy lights feeling. And that’s exactly how the song sounds. There’s a song called ‘Never Grow Up’ that is a song to a little kid who’s asleep in a crib, and it sounds exactly like a lullaby. There’s a song called ‘Mean,’ which was about criticism. And at that time, one of the criticisms I was facing was, ‘She’s not country enough.’ So I was like, ‘Put just as much banjo on this as we can possibly.’ 

	“So when I had learned that, how to match my feelings to really influence what I was writing, and  how I was kind of influencing the production of it to sound exactly the same, it really helped later on when I would be able to write backwards from that. If somebody would send me a track, I’d listen to the first five seconds of the track and be like, ‘Oh my God, this is about a girl who goes home to her hometown on holiday break, and it’s cold, and she falls in love with her old high school flame again, but she has to go back to the big city, but she’s fallen in love with him over the course of two days. What’s she gonna do?'” (The song she’s referring to there, as all Swifties would immediately recognize, is the bittersweet fan favorite “Tis the Damn Season.”)

	Asked by Mason how her lyrical approach changed from her early days being identified as a country artist, Swift says, “I think the main change would be, as a lyricist, just sort of he vernacular over the years that I would use. Because when it comes to writing different shades of my music, you can say the same thing many different ways. You can say ‘I’m into you’ by saying, ‘Your Midas touch on the Chevy door, November flush and your flannel cure.’ Or you can say, ‘You got that James Dean daydream look in your eye.’ They mean exactly the same thing: ‘Everything that you touch glows. You are the most important thing in my world, and I just saw you for the first time, and I can’t believe it, and I don’t know what to do with these feelings.’ But you can just choose to say them different ways.
	

	“And I think that the way that I’ve chosen to express myself as a lyricist has changed over the years, and there are times when like those contradictions will come up where fans will be like, ‘I can’t believe the same person who wrote this wrote this.’ Because one will be very simplistic and silly, and one will be very detailed and deep andwe’re doing tons of allegory, and we’re just in a whole other world of atmospheric speech. But I think that that human contradiction is fun. I think that it’s fun to make playful songs. I think it’s fun to make songs that are desolate and lonely and just bedraggled lyrically as well. And that it’s that human contradiction that I find interesting.”

	The “Reputation” album came up for discussion as a key point in which Swift deliberately played with negative perceptions that were plaguing her and turning them to her music’s advantage. “It was a time in my life when, for the very first time, not the last, people had really actively tried to misunderstand me just in general, and to misunderstand what I was trying to say and to purposely misinterpret it. And it felt very stifling, as a person, as a human being, but ultimately as a writer. It gave me this really, when I look back on it, this really sort of gnarled bite when I would write my lyrics…  This is when I learned, like, when people are in like a hate frenzy about a public figure or really anyone — it could be lyour daughter in her middle school class — when people decide we’re all gonna stand around someone and point and mock them, you can’t respond with outward sincerity. Any attempts you make to explain yourself earnestly or sincerely will just be mocked even worse. And so it was an interesting challenge as a writer to say, ‘What can you possibly say when everything you say is being returned to you in this sort of distorted… like, they overreact rather than react to anything that you say or do, any position you take?’

	“And so I decided to put out a song called ‘Look What You Made Me Do’ as the first single where I, as a dead corpse, emerge from a grave, and then proceed to deliver this very  tongue in cheek, sort of mischievous take on what it’s like to feel cornered in that way. But the fun part of that album is that it had a lot of sides to it. If you looked deeper into that album, it’s an album about feeling so upset about this mass shaming that you felt like you were going through, that you find this little cave, and you crawl in there, and you try to find a tiny bit of warmth, and that warmth sustains you for the entire time that you feel so massively misunderstood by people who don’t know you. … I think the things that I look back on now is, like, when I’ve gone through something that was sort of an attempt to drive me insane, when you don’t allow that to happen, and you use art and music as a way to barrel roll out of that, those are the moments I’m the most proud of.”
	

	But Swift made it clear that she doesn’t think unleavened autobiographical writing is all it’s sometimes cracked up to be in the current world of spill-all-the-tea pop.

	“I think that when I say the term ‘confessional songwriter’… I think it’s important to specify that not all shocking revelations you make about yourself are deep.” There was a pause, as a room full of songwriters — the event was specifically for the Recording Academy’s Songwriters & Composers Wing — erupted into laughter.  “Just saying something dramatic, shocking and wild doesn’t make it something that’s gonna help people, resonate with people, (or) be an important story that sits in people’s minds, hearts and souls. We have to be purposeful. You can’t just cream something crazy and be like, ‘I’m a confessional songwriter.!’ Just for the same exact reason why details should not be strictly decorative. Like, let’s not be haphazard with these things. Let’s make them count.”

	(Watch Swift’s account of how the song “I Knew You Were Trouble” in this video excerpt.)

schema.headline: Taylor Swift Sings Mashup of ‘All Too Well,’ ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ and ‘August’ in Grammy Museum Video

title: Azerbaijan’s Lawyer Defends Defamation Suit Against CNN: ‘These Untrue Statements Actually Put Lives at Risk’
description: Azerbaijan is very upset about a June 5 report on CNN that Israeli troops had used the country as a staging area for attacks on Iran. The country’s
body:
Azerbaijan is very upset about a June 5 report on CNN that Israeli troops had used the country as a staging area for attacks on Iran. The country’s government says that the report, based on anonymous sources, is both completely wrong and dangerous, as it risks drawing Azerbaijan into the conflict.

	In this situation, most governments would issue a condemnatory statement and leave it at that. But Azerbaijan has gone a step farther, filing a defamation suit against CNN in Delaware last week. CNN’s response: “We stand by our reporting.”
	

	The complaint acknowledges that this situation is unusual, and admits that the First Amendment gives Americans the right to criticize their own government without fear of liability. But, it argues that the same logic does not apply to a foreign government, “which is not accountable to the American electorate.”


	To bring the case, Azerbaijan hired Wayne Dennison, a partner at Brown Rudnick who is best known for his work as part of Johnny Depp’s legal team in the case against Amber Heard.

	In an interview, Dennison defended the suit, saying that his client is entitled to recourse for reckless reporting. “These untrue statements actually put lives at risk,” he said.

	This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
	
		It would have been news to me that a foreign government would even think about suing for defamation, or that it would have standing to do that. How is that possible?	

	It’s long been clear that foreign sovereigns have the right to use the U.S. courts to redress harms that have been addressed to them. That’s a fundamental portion of the jurisdiction of our federal courts, and foreign governments have the opportunity to do this. With respect to this case in particular, what we’ve what we’ve looked at is we have a U.S. entity, CNN, engaged in activities that we think are improper and ultimately tortious. And the way in which this government will bring CNN to justice and ultimately to the table is to sue on CNN’s home court. Why’d you bring suit in the U. S.? Because that’s where the defendant is.
	
	
		From the journalism standpoint, obviously there’s a total right to criticize the United States government embedded in the Constitution, right? And I would think that U.S. citizens would also have pretty wide latitude in terms of criticizing foreign governments, too.	

	We’re not talking about criticism. What we’re talking about are direct, factual statements that relate absolutely to an ongoing war. CNN is making statements relative to my clients’ activities in a war that my clients absolutely unequivocally say are untrue. And the result of these untrue statements actually put lives at risk. I know you phrase this in terms of “criticism.” We’re not talking about criticism. What we’re talking about here are statements that — literally the way CNN attributes this is “somebody said,” right? They say “We have an unnamed source.” That is literally nothing more than “somebody said.” And frankly, if what they had reported was “Iranian officials say this,” or “Iran has taken the position that this occurred.” OK, then readers can assess for themselves whether these people are being truthful. But what we have is a report that is nothing other than “somebody said,” and I don’t think you ought to have the umbrella of the First Amendment to protect you from, “Hey, I heard this thing,” especially when you’re in a situation where people may die.
	
		In order to pursue this case, would you have to go get discovery from CNN — like, basically, “Tell me who your sources are.”	

	That may very well be where this ends up. And candidly, part of what you’re talking about here has always been one of the lesser holdings of New York Times v. Sullivan. And I think New York Times v. Sullivan has had some significant questions raised with respect to its continued viability, and this is a Supreme Court that seems far less interested in stare decisis than previous courts.
	
		You think there’s an openness to allowing some government claim of defamation, despite what New York Times v. Sullivan says about that.	

	It’s not the only claim. There’s a prima-facie tort allegation under Delaware law. But the ultimate issue is that we very much expect to be able to go forward and to allege that if your sole reliance as a news organization is on an argument that “somebody said” — and the reporter, with respect to this, has a known history of anti-Azerbaijani reporting — that maybe you got to do a little more, as a news organization.
	
	
		I hear your argument. I would wonder about a chilling effect. Think of foreign dissidents coming to the U.S. and speaking out against their home government. If Iran can come into U.S. courts and sue people who criticize its government, even if what they say is ridiculous and false, it feels like opening a door that you might not want to open.	

	Yeah, and again, I understand the use of the word “criticism.” They made a factual statement that we believe to be — and we believe we can prove to be — untrue. And it’s a factual statement that literally throws an entire country in the middle of a war. At some point, whatever the issue is, you got to look up and say, “Hey, I got to get this right.” I don’t know how to look at it any other way.
	
		If this gets to trial, you will have to show somehow that, in fact, Israeli troops were not staged in Azerbaijan.	

	I assume that they are going to raise as a defense, truth, because that’s a complete defense to defamation. We will then establish that what they reported was untrue, which in fact it was untrue.
	
		You spoke about the peril here. But in terms of the harm suffered, is there a way to quantify the harm to the government of Azerbaijan in terms of dollars from this report?	

	We haven’t made a damages estimate. And candidly, as we proceed, it’s unclear what the damages are going to be. The damages have been very, very significant in terms of international relations. But I can’t tell you to the dollar what the ultimate number is going to be. Frankly, one of the things that we have asked repeatedly from CNN, including in the complaint, is to simply retract the article. And thus far, that that’s been met with either silence or resistance.

schema.headline: Azerbaijan’s Lawyer Defends Defamation Suit Against CNN: ‘These Untrue Statements Actually Put Lives at Risk’

title: Wendy Williams Documentary Series ‘Clap If You Care,’ From the Host’s Longtime TV Producer, Picked Up at Peacock
description: Peacock is digging into the well-mined world of former radio host and TV talk show star Wendy Williams, greenlighting the three-part documentary “Cl
body:
Peacock is digging into the well-mined world of former radio host and TV talk show star Wendy Williams, greenlighting the three-part documentary “Clap If You Care: The Wendy Williams Show” (which is a working title) to air in 2027.

	Williams is not involved in the new docuseries, but her former producer is spearheading the project. As part of its announcement, Peacock confirmed that long-running “The Wendy Williams” show executive producer Susanne Bass, who ran that syndicated strip for 13 seasons, will also executive produce the documentary.
	

	“Her experience brings invaluable insight and a firsthand account of the show’s unique place in pop culture,” the press release said. “Clap If You Care: The Wendy Williams Show” is also executive produced by Ian Orefice, Jon Adler, Amanda Spain and Missy Walker for EverWonder Studio. Chris Witherspoon and Vanessa Golembewski are also EPs. 


	Williams was already a well-known radio star when she launched “The Wendy Williams Show” on TV in 2008. The series ended in June 2022, although the host had taken a leave of absence starting in 2021 due to medical issues related to lymphedema and Graves’ disease.

	The star entered a court-appointed guardianship in 2022, and in 2024, her team disclosed that she had been diagnosed with aphasia (affects language and communication abilities) and frontotemporal dementia, a disorder that impacts behavior and cognitive functions.

	Williams has been vocal about her objections to the guardianships, and her attempts to be removed from it. Just last week, a paparazzi took a video of Williams in New York, where according to the New York Post, she said, “I want out!” as she entered a building. Last year, she called into ABC’s “The View” and told her guardian Sabrina Morrissey and the judge who declared her “legally incapacitated” to “get off my neck,” declaring, “I need a new guardian.” Also last year, she told “The Breakfast Club” radio show that “I feel I’m in a prison” and “I am not cognitively impaired.”
	

	While past documentaries on Williams have focused on her health crises and guardianship, “Clap If You Care” appears to be more focused on the star’s career prior to the end of her show. The doc, according to Peacock, “celebrates the outrageous fun, cultural impact and meteoric rise of ‘The Wendy Williams Show.’”

	Here’s the full logline: “Skyrocketing from unlikely beginnings as a radio host to her impact on entertainment culture, Williams redefined the daytime talk genre with her outrageous on-screen fun on the long-running, Daytime Emmy-nominated talk show. While praising Williams’ TV reign, the documentary also sheds light on the complicated truths about the cost of fame and answers long-lingering questions surrounding the infamous exit from her own show. Over 20 former staffers from the talk show will share their behind-the-scenes experiences and memories of the pop culture icon.”

	Williams was an executive producer on Lifetime’s two-part docuseries “Where Is Wendy Williams?,” which chronicled her decline via footage shot between August 2022 and April 2023. It was a sequel of sorts to Lifetime’s 2021 documentary “Wendy Williams: What A Mess,” which looked at her public divorce and other public mishaps.

schema.headline: Wendy Williams Documentary Series ‘Clap If You Care,’ From the Host’s Longtime TV Producer, Picked Up at Peacock

title: ‘Insidious: Out of the Further’ Director Jacob Chase to Helm Horror Movie ‘Sleepover’ for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal
description: “Insidious: Out of the Further” director Jacob Chase is set to direct the horror project “Sleepover” for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal Pict
body:
“Insidious: Out of the Further” director Jacob Chase is set to direct the horror project “Sleepover” for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal Pictures. Described as the “quintessential sleepover nightmare,” it’s set for an Oct. 8, 2027 theatrical release. 

	Chase directs from a screenplay co-written with “Night Swim” screenwriter Bryce McGuire, adapted from McGuire’s original short story. 


	Blumhouse Atomic Monster also presented Chase’s “Insidious: Out of the Further” along with Sony. The sixth installment in the “Insidious” franchise opened this past weekend to a solid $60 million worldwide. Chase has also directed “Come Play.” 
	

	Ahead of the “Insidious: Out of the Further” release, Chase told Variety, “Scaring people is kind of like magic — literally magic tricks — which is also something I had a real affinity for growing up,” he says. “It’s all misdirection, right? It’s figuring out how you can constantly surprise an audience in the way that the best magic tricks do.”


	Jason Blum will produce, while Chase, McGuire and Bea Sequiera serve as executive producers. Lilly Tyson will oversee the project for Blumhouse Atomic Monster.

	“Sleepover” is a Cinescape Entertainment production presented by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster. 

	Chase is represented by CAA, Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman, and The Initiative Group. McGuire is represented by Gersh and Ziffren Brittenham.

title: ‘Survivor’ vs. ‘The Traitors’: Will Emmy Voters Finally Give the Original Reality Juggernaut Its Due?
description:
“The Traitors” has won more Emmys in three years than “Survivor” has won in 25.

	It’s not close, either. Since arriving on Peacock, Alan Cumming’s
body:
“The Traitors” has won more Emmys in three years than “Survivor” has won in 25.

	It’s not close, either. Since arriving on Peacock, Alan Cumming’s Scottish castle whodunit has banked eight total Emmys — a casting win before it ever cracked the marquee race, back-to-back reality competition trophies in 2024 and 2025, two hosting wins for Cumming and a Creative Arts sweep in 2025 that added cinematography, directing and picture editing in a single cycle. CBS’ long-running “Survivor,” the show that made all of this possible, owns five. That includes Jeff Probst’s four consecutive hosting Emmys from 2008 to 2011 and a 2010 cinematography win. The trophy that matters most, however — outstanding reality-competition program — has eluded it since the Television Academy created the category.
	

	And let’s be clear about why the category exists at all.




	

									Robert Voets/CBS
	



	When “Survivor” premiered in the summer of 2000, it drew 51 million viewers to its season finale, which crowned Richard Hatch the first-ever Sole Survivor. The Academy created the reality competition program Emmy in 2003, in direct response to the boom “Survivor” ignited. Then it handed the inaugural trophy to its CBS sister series “The Amazing Race.” “Survivor” lost to “The Amazing Race” four straight times from 2003 to 2006, before it did something stranger than losing: It completely disappeared.

	For 16 consecutive years, the biggest brand in the genre couldn’t even get nominated — from 2007 through 2022. That stretch included the “Cook Islands” and first Fiji seasons (Seasons 13 and 14), which crowned Yul Kwon — in the first season to feature a final three instead of a final two, a format that coincidentally included Season 50 contestant Ozzy Lusth — and Earl Cole, who became the first unanimous winner in the show’s history.
	

	During that drought, “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” took turns building dynasties. When the new-era “Survivor” finally clawed back into the field in 2023, it lost to “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” It took another year off before returning in 2025, only to lose to “The Traitors.”

	An interesting note is the reality-competition Emmy has gone to a Mark Burnett production four times — all for “The Voice.” The category has spent two decades rewarding the man who helped define the genre while conspicuously never rewarding the show that made him.

	So here we are again, coming off a celebratory 50th season — “In the Hands of the Fans” — that crowned Aubry Bracco over runners-up Jonathan Young and Joe Hunter in an 8-3-0 jury vote and awarded a record-setting $2 million grand prize.

	“The Amazing Race,” a nominee in every eligible year of the category’s existence except the pandemic-scrambled 2020 ceremony, missed the cut entirely for only the second time ever. ABC’s “Dancing with the Stars,” riding its viral resurgence, is back in the race after an 11-year absence, chasing its own 0-for-10 correction.

	The case for “The Traitors” is that it has become the category’s auteur piece.

	Last year’s Creative Arts haul — directing, editing and cinematography — was the TV Academy telling us it doesn’t just enjoy the show; it admires the filmmaking. A third straight win would put it on the most exclusive shelf in reality television, joining “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” as the only shows to three-peat.

	Cumming, meanwhile, is chasing a hosting three-peat of his own, and the man he’d have to beat — for the third year running — is Probst. There’s a whole column in that proxy war alone: the tuxedoed theater lifer with two Tonys against the dimpled adventure guide who won this category’s hosting award the first four times it existed.

	The case for “Survivor” is the one the Emmys sometimes secretly love, and that’s the “overdue” correction.

	This is the Martin Scorsese- “The Departed” scenario — the institution that should have been honored in its prime, finally embraced late, with a milestone providing cover. “Survivor” hit Season 50 this spring, a fan-voted celebration of a quarter-century on CBS, exactly the kind of legacy moment that lets a voter feel like they’re honoring history rather than simply a season of television.
	

	Probst has spent the year as the genre’s beloved elder statesman. If there was ever a cycle for sentiment to beat momentum, it’s a 50th-season cycle.

	But sentiment has to overcome a structural problem: This category does not do lifetime achievement. It does dynasties.

	In 23 previous ceremonies, it has crowned exactly seven different shows. And once it falls for something, it falls hard — seven straight for “The Amazing Race,” four in five years for “The Voice,” four straight for “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” Television Academy voters — and this is a category voted on by the entire membership, rather than a specific peer group — aren’t correctors; they’re serial monogamists.



	

					THE TRAITORS — “The Death Conga” Episode 402 — Pictured: (l-r) Caroline Stanbury, Colton Underwood, Rob Rausch, Johnny Weir, Maura Higgins, Tiffany Mitchell, Candiace Dillard Basset — (Photo by: Euan Cherry/Peacock)
									Euan Cherry/Peacock
	



	Right now, they’re in love with a castle in the Scottish Highlands.

	Did enough of the all-stars fighting it out on the islands of Fiji build enough goodwill to get “Survivor” across the finish line?

	“Survivor” has outlasted every rival, every trend and every obituary written for network television. The one thing it has never figured out how to outlast is Emmy voters’ attraction to the newest game in town — a lesson it has now been taught by three different shows across three different decades.

	The torch, as Probst would say, represents life in the game. “Survivor” has kept its lit for 25 years — and will light a new one again this fall.

	On Sept. 14, we find out whether the Academy finally notices — or whether the castle drawbridge stays up for one more year. Voting closes Aug. 26 at 10 p.m. PT.

	This week’s updated Emmy winner predictions are below.

title: NBA Player Brandon Clarke Had White Powder, Narcan, Syringes in Home When He Died
description:
Memphis Grizzlies' Brandon Clarke
                          White Powder, Narcan & Syringes Found
body:
Memphis Grizzlies' Brandon Clarke
                          White Powder, Narcan & Syringes Found at Home
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 24, 2026
                
                            1:27 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 24, 2026
                                3:12 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Brandon Clarke had an unknown white powder, Narcan, syringes and a slew of medications inside his home when he was found dead ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's report, investigators found vape devices, cannabis products, prescription medications, injectable peptides, syringes and a box of Narcan inside Clarke's bedroom and attached bathroom.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Investigators also found a plate containing an unknown white powdery substance on the kitchen island ... along with a hotel key card.
      

            TMZ broke the story ... Clarke was found unresponsive in bed at his Los Angeles-area home in May, and the medical examiner later ruled his death an accident caused by the effects of heroin and cocaine, with multiple prescription medications contributing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The report says there were no apparent signs of foul play or fatal injuries at the scene.
      
    
            Clarke's agent had been trying to reach him that day ... and eventually asked his housemate to go check on him.
      
    
            The housemate went into Clarke's bedroom and found him unresponsive in bed before calling 911. Investigators noted bright bloody purge residue on the bedsheets and pillows.
      
    
            His housemate also told investigators the 29-year-old had a history of drug use ... including previous stints in rehab.
      
    
            Clarke spent his entire seven-year NBA career in Memphis ... after the Grizzlies landed him as a first-round pick in 2019. He was only 29.

                                  August 24, 2026

            Kim Richards was spotted in a rare public sighting months after her eviction drama with sister Kyle Richards ... spending time near the beach in Santa Monica ... and looking none too pleased.
      
    
            TMZ obtained a photo of "The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" alum sitting on a park bench near the Santa Monica Pier Friday ... wearing a cowboy hat and a loose red dress, with one tan boot on and her other foot bare.
      
    
            It looks like Kim is painting something in the pic.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            While the photo may raise questions about Kim's living situation, sources familiar with the situation tell TMZ she's not homeless. We're told Kyle helped Kim secure a place in the Santa Monica area near the beach.
      

            Other sources connected to the family tell us Kim continues to have her ups and downs. Her daughters still live in Los Angeles, and we're told she spends time with them.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported, Kyle sued Kim in January 2025, seeking to have her older sister vacate Kyle's 2-bedroom Encino condo after telling her to move out in late 2024.
      
    
            Kim never responded to the lawsuit, and a default judgment was entered in March 2025 requiring her to surrender the property. Court docs later showed the L.A. County Sheriff's Office tried to serve Kim with the judgment in June, but she'd already moved out, allowing Kyle to take possession.
      
    
            The lawsuit came months after sources told us Kim had relapsed following years of addiction issues, prompting her family to take a "tough love" approach.
      
    
            Kyle and Kathy Hilton later said during the 'RHOBH' Season 14 reunion that Kim was living in Florida and "doing better."
